title: Burst shepherding & spotlight shed playbook for quota gatekeepers
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Summary: In the last two incidents, a combination of regional network flaps and a hot burst workload caused our central quota-enforcement layer to enter a slow path, resulting in 15–30 minute SLO breaches for p95 tail latency and an increase in token cost due to unbounded retries. This ticket defines a robust operational and technical playbook — 'burst shepherding' + 'spotlight shed' — to make quota gatekeepers resilient to bursts, fair across tenants, and safe during limiter outages.

Goals and success criteria:
- Prevent cross-tenant cascading failure during short bursts while preserving p95/p99 latency SLOs for priority traffic.
- Ensure graceful degradation mode completes within 5 seconds and reduces load to stable level within 60s.
- Provide clear onboarded metrics and runbook steps for on-call to recover from limiter outages.
- Can be rolled out via canary in two regions with automated fallback to current behavior.

Background and rationale:
Current admission layer centralizes token credits and tries to be fair by strict per-tenant windows. During large bursts or when the admission coordinator hits a GC/heap pause or DB hiccup, requests queue up, timers drift, and we end up either accepting too many low-value requests (cost blowout) or blocking heavy workloads (high customer impact). Existing solutions (token-leaky approaches, tenant draining) either prioritize throughput or equity, but not both during outages.

Design overview (high level):
1) Burst shepherding: short-lived, local admission reservoir attached to each proxy that buffers small bursts (configurable reservoir secs, default 8s) and applies a decaying credit algorithm. Reservoirs are filled from long-term quota but can temporarily overdraw only a bounded amount to absorb spikes without hitting the central coordinator.
2) Spotlight shed: when the central quota backend becomes unavailable or latency/cpu cross SLO thresholds, the proxy switches to a shed policy that prioritizes 'spotlight' traffic: high-signal requests (internal health checks, paid-tier customer routes, user-interactive tokens with low latency SLA). Spotlight selection is a deterministic scoring function: route priority + recent success rate + tenant SLA weight. Non-spotlight traffic is probabilistically rejected with an exponential backoff window tuned per-tenant.
3) Circuit breaker + fast rejoin: proxies implement a soft circuit that trips on coordinator latency/failed lease ratio > 5% for 10s. On trip, proxies enter Spotlight shed and periodically probe the coordinator with low-rate health probes. Rejoin occurs after 3 consecutive successful probes with stable latency.
4) Fairness reclamation: a background reconciler gradually reclaims borrowed reservoir credits using a best-effort reclamation quorum to avoid long-term overdraw for a small number of tenants.

Trade-offs considered:
- Strong fairness (strict global counters) vs availability: we accept bounded temporary unfairness to stay available.
- Complexity of cross-proxy consensus for reservoirs vs operational simplicity: we keep reservoirs local and rely on later reconciliation rather than synchronous coordination.
- Deterministic shedding vs randomized shedding: mixing deterministic spotlight selection for high-value traffic with randomized probability for bulk traffic helps mitigate adversarial burst patterns.

Telemetry and observability:
- New Grafana dashboard panel: limiter.reservoir.borrow_rate, limiter.spotlight_accept_rate, limiter.shed_rate_by_tenant, limiter.coordinator_latency_p95, limiter.trip_count. Link: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/limiter/burst-shepherding (placeholder).
- SLOs to watch during rollout: p95 latency (API user-facing) and error-rate for paid-tier routes.
- Postmortem fields: include reservoir_overdraw_owners and reconcile_duration in incident report.

Testing and verification:
- Unit tests for scoring and reservoir accounting.
- Integration tests simulate coordinator read/write failures and verify correct switch to shed mode and rejoin behavior.
- Chaos tests: GRPC/HTTP delay injection and region partitioning runs in staging with the chaos harness (linked below).
- Load test matrix: burst sizes (2x, 5x, 10x normal), tenant skew (top-10 tenants at 60% traffic), and long tail requests.

Rollout plan:
1) Feature-flagged deploy to canary in us-west-2 with conservative reservoir sizes and spotlight whitelist for internal traffic only.
2) Monitor telemetry for 72 hours; automated rollback if paid-tier error-rate increases by >0.2% or p95 latency regresses >15%.
3) Expand to eu-west-1 and run cross-region failover test (induce coordinator unavailability in one region and verify other region's proxies handle spotlight shed correctly).
4) Full rollout with opt-in tenant trial and docs.

Operational playbook (quick):
- Detection: Alert on coordinator_latency_p95 > 500ms for 30s or trip_count > 0.
- Immediate mitigation: flip FF:burst_shepherding.enable=true (enables reservoirs) and if coordinator unresponsive, enable FF:spotlight_shed.force=true to protect high-value routes.
- Recovery: monitor probe_success_rate; once stable for 3 minutes, clear force flag and allow normal reconciliation.

Documentation & links:
- Design doc (Confluence): https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/123456/Burst+Shepherding+Design
- Implementation PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/12345
- Chaos test harness job: https://ci.redwood.ai/job/chaos/limiter-burst-shepherding
- Grafana dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/limiter/burst-shepherding

Open questions & TBDs:
- Exact reservoir sizing per region under mixed workloads (need load experiments).
- Whether to persist short-lived borrowing tokens to allow cross-proxy fast reconciliation after regional failover. Persisting increases complexity and write amplification.
- Long-term: integrate with quota billing to charge for borrowed credits if borrow window > 5m.

Next steps (this ticket covers):
- Finalize scoring function and FF surface (Asha).
- Implement proxy-side reservoir and circuit (Marcus).
- Add telemetry panels and automated alerts (Riley).
- Run chaos and load tests; prepare canary rollout (Diego).
